title: Do lobbyists and donors buy votes, access or information?
text: What is unknown is which channel actually moves policy: transmitting information to legislators, buying access, or buying votes outright. The field has well-developed models of informational lobbying and a few empirical tests, but no setting that separates the channels, and the multi-round, multi-expert and dynamic versions are untouched.
why: The information passed to politicians and their informational needs are unobserved, and informational and electoral effects of contributions are intertwined in the same data.

title: How much policy does lobbying buy, and at what welfare cost?
text: What is unknown is the causal return to lobbying spending and contributions (policy won, firm value) and how far lobbying-shaped equilibrium policies sit from the social optimum. Structural estimates exist for trade protection and energy, but pre-legislative effects, wins that merely preserve the status quo, and other policy domains are unmeasured.
why: No design isolates lobbying's causal effect on outcomes, much of what lobbying wins is an invisible continuation of the status quo, and the no-lobbying counterfactual needed to price distortions is never observed.

title: What makes some organised interests win: size, structure or rivals?
text: Which groups actually get their demands met, and why, is unknown: group size and concentration, form of organisation, opposition from rival lobbies, or members' wealth (the merely affluent versus the top 0.1 percent). Classic theory (Olson, Becker, Stigler, Peltzman) and correlational evidence on elites exist, but group power is still treated as a taste parameter.
why: Data linking specific groups' demands to outcomes are scarce (so far mostly case studies), and no design separates group size from organisation and rivalry.

title: How is influence organised: lobbying firms, coalitions and networks?
text: What is unknown is how the supply of influence is structured: whether firms lobby alone, in coalitions or through hired firms, how lobbying firms are organised and compete, and how groups spread resources across socially connected legislators and across local and national levels. Lobbying research has mostly modelled and measured how much is spent, not who delivers it.
why: Lobbying-firm, client, coalition and legislator-network data have only recently been assembled, and theory has centred on the amount of lobbying rather than its organisation.

title: Do limits on political money curb influence or just divert it?
text: Unknown is what spending limits, firm-donation bans, Citizens United, disclosure and revolving-door cooling-off periods do to policy, corruption and the use of other channels (lobbying, dark money, charity, shadow lobbying). Discontinuity work now shows effects on elections and donor types, but downstream policy outcomes and substitution are mostly untested.
why: Reform thresholds identify only local effects on elections, and the covert channels that rules may push money into are unrecorded by design.

title: Do survey-measured persuasion effects survive real campaigns?
text: Unknown is whether persuasion and advertising effects estimated in survey experiments and short field tests persist to Election Day and carry over to competitive campaigns, micro-targeted media and non-US party systems. Field experiments find small average effects, but studies differ in design and setting, and survey-based message testing predicts real effects poorly.
why: Strategic opponents, repeated exposure and whole-campaign strategies cannot be randomised, and survey and field estimates have not been matched on the same treatments.

title: What drives regulators' enforcement choices, and who gets leniency?
text: Unknown is how far regulators and enforcers deviate from the rules in applying them, what drives the deviation (donations, capacity, personal discretion, citizen pressure) and what it costs in outcomes. Evidence from US banking, Indian pollution inspections, Chinese pollution appeals and Colombian deforestation shows enforcement varies, but each study covers one industry or country.
why: Enforcement effort and its outcomes (ambient air, water, forest) are rarely observed directly, so discretion must be inferred from noisy outcomes or one-off experiments.

title: What is a person's total news diet across platforms and devices?
text: What is unknown is how much news individuals consume in total, from which titles and through which devices, because existing work studies one platform at a time and no public dataset follows the same people across newspapers, television and online. The field has platform-specific effects and shares, but cannot say how large media power is outside the biggest outlets.
why: Consumption surveys do not identify titles, browsing and app data sit with platforms, and stories seen on feeds but not read or remembered go unrecorded.

title: Do media-driven shifts in beliefs and votes last and change policy?
text: What is unknown is whether media-induced changes in beliefs and votes persist beyond a year and show up in what governments do and in welfare, not only in turnout or vote shares. Short-run effects on votes and some on public spending are documented, but only four of fifteen reviewed persuasion studies cover horizons of a year or longer, and policy links are mostly inferred.
why: Outcomes that matter for welfare (policy choices, official performance) are measured coarsely, and long-run follow-up of media exposure is rarely possible.

title: Does competition and entry of rival outlets discipline media bias?
text: What is unknown is whether more rival senders, outlets or narratives reduce distortion: whether an ideologically distinct entrant pulls incumbents toward or away from the centre, whether alternative sources discipline reputation-driven bias, and whether viewers switch away when choice exists. Theory yields competition results that depend on commitment, but empirical tests are scarce.
why: Entry and the availability of alternatives are rarely exogenous, and reputation-driven bias cannot be told apart from consumer, reporter or government tastes for distortion.

title: Do internet effects on protest and votes survive 4G and closed states?
text: What is unknown is whether the participation, protest and populist-voting effects found for early broadband, 2G phones and first-generation social media still hold with 3G/4G, smartphones and very fast broadband, in tightly controlled media environments, and through which behavioural channels. Mobile coverage, broadband and social media shift mobilisation and votes in particular settings (Manacorda and Tesei 2020, Campante et al. 2017, Guriev et al. 2019, Qin et al. 2021), but each estimate is one technology generation in one country.
why: Each design exploits a single rollout, individual-level usage data are missing so user and non-user channels cannot be separated, and no data allow a systematic test of what content drives the effect.

title: Do audiences discount slanted news, and is persuasion really learning?
text: What is unknown is how receivers weigh sender incentives and discount biased information, and whether persuasion works through belief updating, hardened conviction or self-persuasion, which also decides who is moved. Reduced-form studies measure average vote and belief shifts (DellaVigna and Kaplan 2007, Gentzkow et al. 2011), while models of incomplete discounting and misspecified inference lack direct estimates (Knight and Tribin-Uribe 2018, Bowen et al. 2023).
why: Reduced-form designs deliver averages over many markets and events, so heterogeneity and mechanisms stay unidentified without direct tests of the persuasion models.

title: Do fact-checks and corrections change votes and actions, not beliefs?
text: What is unknown is whether corrections and fact-checks move actual votes and behaviour rather than stated beliefs, which design choices make them work, how much measured misperception is partisan cheerleading, and whether misinformation is really more prevalent than in the past. Surveys and experiments document fake-news exposure and belief updating after corrections (Allcott and Gentzkow 2017, Nyhan et al. 2019, Jerit and Zhao 2020), but nobody has estimated how persuasive false stories are relative to ordinary campaign ads.
why: Corrections are tested in one-shot online experiments on stated beliefs, exposure on feeds is unrecorded, and there is no historical baseline against which to judge whether misperception has risen.

title: What do states gain from buying or censoring news, and what curbs it?
text: What is unknown is how much state ownership, government advertising and censorship actually move beliefs and votes (the price of a vote bought through the press), and which reforms, outside sources or institutional checks undo capture. Government pressure on coverage and censorship effects are documented in single regimes (Qian and Yanagizawa-Drott 2017, Chen and Yang 2019, Szeidl and Szucs 2021) and capture models predict reform effects (Besley and Prat 2006), but nearly all persuasion evidence comes from democracies.
why: Capture, ownership and advertising are chosen by the regimes being studied, outlets' and readers' preferences cannot be separated from state pressure, and few settings offer credible variation in access to non-state information.

title: Which channel carries economic and climate shocks into violence?
text: What is unknown is which channel turns income, price, harvest and climate shocks into conflict (a lower opportunity cost of fighting, loot to capture, grievance, a weaker state), and whether the relationship survives warming, non-agrarian economies and new population or commodity shocks. Rainfall, commodity-price and climate studies show that conflict responds to shocks (Miguel et al. 2004, Dube and Vargas 2013, Hsiang et al. 2013), but they identify a reduced form rather than the margin that moves.
why: Competing channels (opportunity cost, rapacity, grievance, state weakness) predict the same reduced form, and the intermediate variables that would separate them, such as inequality, hunger and grievances, are unmeasured at fine scale.

title: Which aid, job and security policies cut violence, and which backfire?
text: What is unknown is which programmes (food and military aid, development projects, cash, jobs, therapy) lower rather than raise violence, why aid studies disagree, and whether effects last past a programme's early stage or travel to other countries. Food aid raises conflict in some settings (Nunn and Qian 2012), community development projects often leave security unchanged or give insurgents targets (Beath et al. 2016, Beath et al. 2025), and jobs, cash and therapy for high-risk men have been tested in few trials (Blattman and Annan 2016, Blattman et al. 2017).
why: Effects hinge on how projects are managed, who captures them and whether insurgents rely on local support, none of which is measured consistently across studies, and project-level conflict data are scarce.

title: Does war come from information, commitment, power shifts or identity?
text: What is unknown is which mechanisms (private information, commitment problems, shifts in relative power, domestic politics, identity) account for actual wars and how they combine within one conflict, and what microfoundations generate the power shifts and antagonisms that models take as given. Rationalist bargaining theory is well developed (Fearon 1995, Powell 2004, Powell 2006) and ethnic-conflict models separate economic from primordial antagonisms (Esteban et al. 2012), but power shifts enter as exogenous or reduced-form (Powell 2013) and Fearon found no case of leaders updating on capabilities.
why: Single-mechanism models are tractable but real wars mix information, commitment and identity, and the power shifts and antagonisms they turn on are rarely observed, so mechanisms are hard to tell apart empirically.

title: How do armed groups, gangs and mafias form, recruit and govern?
text: What is unknown is how violent non-state organisations come into being, recruit, ally and govern, and by which exact channels they shape local government, corruption and development. Studies show mafias intimidate politicians, trade favours with them and affect development (Acemoglu et al. 2017, Alesina et al. 2018, De Feo and De Luca 2017), but corruption, other crime and reduced competition cannot be separated, and data on insurgent, militia and drug-trade organisations are thin.
why: Such groups leave little evidence, their internal organisation and cross-alliances are latent, and the available strategies cannot separate the channels through which they matter.

title: Does counterterrorism end violence or feed mobilisation?
text: What is unknown is whether crackdowns, drone strikes, defences and counterterror laws end terror campaigns or raise mobilisation and splintering, how insurgents adapt to them, and what terrorists want (concessions or a harsh response). Models and short-run evidence exist (de Mesquita and Dickson 2007, Benmelech et al. 2014, Rigterink 2020), but whether counterterror was a main cause of any campaign's end is untested beyond short horizons.
why: Terrorist goals and internal control are unobserved, insurgents substitute across tactics so measured effects are short-lived, and evidence comes from a handful of theatres.

title: When do protests change policy, and what makes people keep joining?
text: What is unknown is which mechanisms turn protest into policy, opinion and vote change (agenda-setting versus roll-call stage, violent versus nonviolent tactics), and how individuals' decisions to join interact (strategic substitutes or complements, free-riding, social ties, friendship). Single-movement studies find protest moves votes (Madestam et al. 2013) and participation models treat joining as a coordination or substitution game (Cantoni et al. 2019, Barbera and Jackson 2020), but the mechanisms and their generality across movements are untested.
why: Prior work pools violent and nonviolent tactics and aggregates by year and state, so effects are rarely identified separately, and the data cannot separate competing mechanisms.

title: How long do violence and trauma mark local economies and preferences?
text: What is unknown is how persistent the damage from war, riots, terrorism and criminal violence is for local economies and human capital, and whether exposure shifts political and social preferences through individual trauma or inherited community memory. Bombing studies show quick recovery in some local economies (Davis and Weinstein 2002, Miguel and Roland 2010) and exposure shifts cooperation and political engagement in others (Bauer et al. 2016, Blattman 2009), but mechanisms and generality beyond single countries are thin.
why: The no-conflict counterfactual is hard to construct, exposure is measured at the area rather than the individual level, and long-run follow-up of exposed people is rare.
